The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers by Paul Kennedy Randall Baker, the reviewer, is a pro- fessor in the Indiana University School of Public and Environmental Affairs. We don't want to fight, But by jingo if we do, We've got the ships, We've got the men, We've got the money too! T his little ditty, made popular in Kipling's era when Great Britain controlled one-quarter of the globe, summarizes the central theme of Paul Kennedy's book, The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers: the military might of any great power, or confederation of powers, rests ultimately on its eco- nomic capacity--relative to its rivals-- to sustain that posture. Kennedy ex- amines the concept by encyclopedic study of a period extending from Habsburg Spain and Austria through post-World War II U.S./USSR bipo- larism. What differentiates this work from other studies of Great Power ri- valry (and ensures its hot pursuit by the media) is the inclusion of a final chapter projecting the lessons of the past into the future, continuing what Bismark called the "stream of time." What this last section contains will not really be news for any informed reader. But following, as they do, 500 pages of meticulous research, these prognostications and projections come in a context of authority and conti- nuity. "'Kennedy's hypothesis concentrates not on the absolute numbers of soldiers or ships but on the relative economic strength of any power." Kennedy's hypothesis concen- trates not on the absolute numbers of soldiers or ships but on the relative economic strength of any power. He sees an historic contradiction be- tween short-term military preoccu- pations and the long-term economic strengths needed to sustain power (a concept he terms "global over- reach"). Thus, for instance, the costs of policing the British Empire even- tuaUy exceeded the rate of new wealth creation the Empire needed to sustain its dominating role in the face of such rising giants as Germany, the United States, Japan, and others. What is sig- nificant, Kennedy notes, is the late phase of Great Power status, when the declining Great Powers' econ- omies fail to match up globally with their rising counterparts. Then there is a tendency to retrench on the de- fense side to prevent history rather than to increase economic investment and move with the tide more realist- ically. So the "relative decline" period is one fraught with dangers if a de- clining power weakens its relative

84 Business Horizons / November-December 1988 economic capacity and builds up its defenses to unsustainable levels. It is then left vulnerable; weakened, ex- posed, and unable to perform the role it wishes to retain. It is easy to see why this book has had such a broad press reception in the United States; it puts spiraling de- fense budgets, budget deficits, debts and borrowing, SDI, and protection- ism in a context stretching back to Philip II's Spain. Kennedy's message is that the United States must learn how to work within a framework of relative decline and secure its eco- nomic strength, not operate in the bi- polar conditions of the immediate post-War era, the Truman Doctrine, and global domination of trade, gold reserves, and .military strength. The commitments from an earlier time can very easily continue to weaken the very economic base that gave the U.S. such power in the 30 years after 1945. One complication that might seem to insert an historical discontinuity into Kennedy's 500-year thesis is the advent of nuclear weapons, which appear to upset the old formula of men, guns, ships, and (recently) planes. He states, however, that the nuclear card is essentially unplayable; there is just as much need to consider "conventional" options as there ever was, and their costs have risen astro- nomically. The nuclear bill, in es- sence, gets added on top, and with SDI around the corner the total bill threatens to climb out of sight. This seems to reinforce the author's ar- gument that short-term defense con- siderations take precedence over long- run economic strengths. Furthermore, by Kennedy's reck- oning, the world of the future will be a much more complicated place than de Tocqueville's predicted two-su- perpower world. With both the U.S. and the USSR declining steadily rel- ative to other parts of the world, power in the future will be geograph- ically much less concentrated. We have the extraordinary economic rise to world status of Japan, a country that has by today's terms minimal de- fense commitments--thus freeing up even more funds for economic de- velopment. But what of the Japan of the future? History seems to have no precedent for such dominance in one arena but not in the other. If its rel- ative decline forces the U.S. out of its supportive defense presence in (and, maybe, into a trade war with) Japan, how would that country's rearma- ment be viewed in China? Then there is the EEC, which has enormous mil- itary and economic might but is not a state at all. Parts of it are members of NATO, parts are not, parts are neu- tral. The impossibility of predicting just how this giant will move toward political sovereignty and a common defense posture raises extraordinary questions about NATO and about Eu- rope's front-line position in the U.S. defense strategy against the Soviets in the West. Again the relative decline of the U.S. may accelerate moves to- ward removing troops and material from Europe; again there is the grow- ing possibility of trade conflicts over a share of the global market. Kennedy regards China as a sleep- ing giant. Despite its enormous size and its ability to mobilize millions of troops, it remains economically very poor relative to the other powers. In addition, the present policy of the "Four Modernizations" has reduced the resources made available to the Peo- ple's Liberation Army. However, if that country sustains its post-1978 growth and realizes its potential, then China would have the economic base to be a global force, and this possi- bility concerns both Japan and the USSR in the first case renewing fears I of Japanese regional dominance, and in the other adding to the starvation of the Soviet economy through ex- cessive additional defense costs. "'Kennedy's lesson is that the U.S. should accept its relative decline and cast alliances and economic policies accordingly something that has received little enough attention in this election year.'" Kennedy's lesson is that the U.S. should accept its relative decline and cast alliances and economic policies accordingly--something that has re- ceived little enough attention in elec- tion year. The U.S. cannot police the free world any longer. In this context, embryonic trade disputes and un- bending, simplistic defense postures may well alienate Japan, China, and the EEC, whose role may be to take up some of the American slack. Brit- ain has shown how difficult it is for a country to give up hegemony and grandeur. Kennedy's book encour- ages us to learn from and move with history rather than to try to prevent change. Orthodox historians may de- cry this speculative futurology, but it ensures that more people from a wider field will read this tour de force. Jin- goism is no substitute for reality. [] Paul Kennedy, The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers. New York. Random House, 1987. 677 pp. $24.95.
